subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
passage: I'm Francis, and last week I kept getting subtraction sums wrong. I guessed a lot, and guessing did not help. One evening I took a sheet and wrote exactly where I got lost: "When the top digit is smaller, I don't know the borrowing." Papa read it and said, "That's my boy. Now you know the exact spot." Next day I showed Ira Ma'am the line. "Can you show me just this step again?" She did not do the whole page. She showed me one sum, breaking a ten into ones, and then she let me try the next. I got it right. I wrote her a thank-you note.

qa.q: What step of subtraction did Francis find hard?
qa.a: He got lost at the borrowing step, when the top digit is smaller.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling after Ira Ma'am let him try the next sum himself?
qa.a: He felt pleased and relieved when he got it right. He was so glad that he wrote her a thank-you note.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Francis use to practise borrowing after class, and why?
qa.a: He could do five borrowing sums at home and mark each himself. Repeating that one step will make it feel normal.

qa.q: How might Ira Ma'am see Francis's question?
qa.a: Ira Ma'am probably finds it easy to help, because Francis asked about one exact step instead of saying he did not understand anything.

grounding: A child notices guessing does not help, writes down that he gets lost at the borrowing step, and next day asks the teacher to show that one step.

subtype: Approach: asking the teacher a specific question [Revision]
passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. For a week Kishore has been guessing at subtraction and getting a different answer each time. Today he came to my desk with a torn slip of paper. On it he had written: 'I get lost in the borrowing step, when the top number is smaller.' Then: 'Can you show only that part again?' I did, with bundles of ten sticks, breaking one bundle open when the ones ran out. He did 52 − 27 at my desk and got 25. Sachin, who was hovering nearby, asked if he could watch too. Kishore's slip is going on the wall as an example of a good question.

qa.q: What did Kishore write on the slip of paper?
qa.a: 'I get lost in the borrowing step, when the top number is smaller.'

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling when he brought the slip to the desk?
qa.a: He was probably a little nervous but determined, after a week of frustrating guesses.

qa.q: What made Kishore's question work so well?
qa.a: It named the exact step, borrowing, so the teacher could show just that part instead of the whole topic again.

qa.q: How does the note-writer see Kishore's slip?
qa.a: The note-writer sees it as a model of a good question and is putting it on the wall for others.

grounding: Shows a child who notices guessing isn't working, writes down that the borrowing step is where he gets lost, and asks the teacher to show that step.

passage:
Friday
For days I've been guessing on subtraction. 403 minus 168, and a new answer every time. Last night I did one sum very slowly and wrote down where my head went blank. It was the same place every time: the 3 on top is smaller than the 8, and next door is a 0, so where do I borrow from? I wrote in the back of my notebook: 'Borrowing across a zero: please show again.' Today I gave it to Sir. He did just that step on the board, twice. 403 − 168 = 235. I got it. Imran had said just copy his answers, but Mummy said, 'Harish beta, copying won't sit the exam for you.'

qa.q: What did Harish write in the back of his notebook?
qa.a: 'Borrowing across a zero: please show again.'

qa.q: How did Harish feel about the days of guessing?
qa.a: Harish seemed frustrated at getting a new answer each time, which pushed him to find exactly where he got lost.

qa.q: Why did writing down the stuck step help more than guessing?
qa.a: It pinned down the one step, borrowing across a zero, so Sir could show just that instead of the whole topic.

qa.q: How might Sir see Harish's note?
qa.a: Sir can see exactly what to teach and did that step twice on the board, so he likely appreciated such a clear question.

grounding: Illustrates a boy who stops guessing, writes down that borrowing across a zero is where he gets lost, and asks the teacher to show that step again.
